newsitem.title: USA: Clinton rues FBI failure to warn him on China.
newsitem.headline: Clinton rues FBI failure to warn him on China.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Monday he was kept in the dark about an FBI warning last year that China might try to funnel money into the U.S. election campaign, and is now trying to find out why.

Clinton also said allegations China sought to meddle in U.S. politics "would be very serious if it were true," but urged people not to jump to conclusions, saying it was important to first determine if the FBI suspicions were valid.
"Let's find out what the truth is if we can," he said.

Earlier on Monday, White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters the FBI warned two intelligence specialists at the National Security Council (NSC) last June of a suspected Chinese plan to "funnel money to congressional candidates", but asked the officials not to tell higher-ups.
His disclosure added a bizarre new twist to a campaign financing controversy dogging Clinton and his Democratic Party, and one with potentially troubling and sensitive foreign policy implications.

It is illegal for foreign governments to contribute to U.S. political campaigns. Mounting allegations that there were such efforts raise questions as to whether the objective was to buy influence over U.S. foreign and trade policy decisions.

Clinton said he had not been aware of the FBI's suspicions "during the election period last year", when he was re-elected president. Had he known, he said, he would have asked for them to be investigated.

"Yes I believe I should have known. No I didn't know. If I had known, I would have asked the NSC and the chief of staff to look at the evidence and make whatever recommendations were appropriate," he told a news conference.

"This is a very serious allegation. But as far as I know, it is only that," the president said. He added that it would be a "foolish error" for any foreign power to try to sway the outcome of a U.S. election.

"Anyone who understands the sort of interplay of American politics, the scope and scale of the issues, the amount of investment involved, I mean it would just not make very much sense," said Clinton, who seemed philosophical about not being told about the FBI warning at the time it was given.
When a reporter suggested that he did not seem angry and asked him why, Clinton replied: ""Well, what I seem and what I feel may be two different things.
"The older I get the more I become aware of the fact that there's some things there's no point of expending a lot of energy on. It didn't happen. It should have happened. It was a mistake," he said.
Since the election the Democratic Party has returned nearly $3 million to donors -- most with links to Asian businesses or governments -- that were deemed questionable.

Allegations of Chinese plans to interfere in U.S. politics, which first surfaced in a Washington Post report on Feb. 13, threatened to disturb a thaw in Chinese-American relations that began last year after a long period of estrangement.

Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat, said at a news conference she had been warned by the FBI as early as 1991 about possible Chinese government contributions to U.S. campaigns, and again last June.

At the latter meeting, she said, "These efforts included possible Chinese government efforts to funnel money to congressional campaigns through intermediaries. The FBI also stated that the (Chinese) Ministry of State Security indicated its support to influence campaigns."
China has called the charges unfounded and said on Monday it had lodged a protest with the United States.
"The Chinese side has never got involved in U.S. political affairs in any form," the official Xinhua news agency quoted a senior Chinese foreign ministry official as saying.
McCurry said that had the administration known about the alleged Chinese effort to curry favour with U.S. leaders it "might have acted diplomatically" to discourage this.
He said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had raised the issue with Chinese leaders during a recent Beijing visit.
The latest turn in the ongoing Clinton campaign financing controversy came as pressure mounted on Attorney General Janet Reno to name an independent counsel to investigate the flap.
Committees in both houses of Congress are working on probes into various aspects of the issue.
